alternative: Let the GC own object lifetime: release unmanaged resources deterministically with IDisposable/using (IAsyncDisposable/await using on async paths), wrap native handles in SafeHandle - which maintains its own internal reference count (DangerousAddRef/DangerousRelease) so a handle survives a call in flight - and keep AddRef/Release only where a COM/WinRT boundary demands it; WeakReference and ConditionalWeakTable cover caches and side associations.
idiom_name: none - GC owns lifetime; SafeHandle/IDisposable at the native boundary
implementation_notes: The CLR decides liveness by tracing reachability, not by counting: a field incremented on copy would claim a lifetime it cannot control, because the object is reclaimed when no root references it no matter what the field says. What replaces the classic structure: using/Dispose for deterministic release of unmanaged resources, SafeHandle for native handles - the runtime gives it an internal reference count (DangerousAddRef/DangerousRelease) precisely so a P/Invoke in flight cannot race its release - and AddRef/Release only at COM/WinRT boundaries where the foreign protocol owns the count. Finalizers are not a substitute: they run on the finalizer thread at a time the GC chooses, can resurrect the object and extend at least one collection.
pitfalls: Finalizers and ReleaseHandle run at the GC's discretion: never make correctness depend on when they run, and never touch objects that can resurrect the dying instance from them.
A SafeHandle must not be closed manually while an asynchronous P/Invoke is still in flight; DangerousAddRef exists to hold the count across exactly that window.
A COM RCW keeps a runtime-managed AddRef/Release count; releasing it from a non-owning reference, or twice, decrements a count the runtime still depends on.
